However, if a large subperiosteal abscess (>10 mm) or orbital abscess is present, or if nerve and vascular compromise are present, surgical intervention may be necessary.[1]

snippets.text: The most common complications of orbital cellulitis involve abscess formation, specifically subperiosteal abscesses. These are most commonly seen involving the medial wall or floor of the orbit, as they are the thinnest orbital components. Orbital abscesses, however rare, are still possible and can cause persistent fever despite 48 hours of IV antibiotics.[1][3]

snippets.text: Disposition from acute care settings depends on the extent of infection, comorbidities, and access to prompt ophthalmological follow-up. Uncomplicated or chronic cases must be advised proper treatment and require adequate follow-up. Acute or complicated cases need an urgent ophthalmology consult and possible inpatient admission for further management. Complications of dacryocystitis, though devastating, can be managed with timely intravenous antibiotics and necessary surgical interventions.
